title: The verse explained
hook: Ananda, Mahakaccana and Lomasakangiya each explain the same verse

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhaddekaratta, one fine night, a short verse about living where you are. Your line: see it clearly, right where it is.
screen: `SEE IT CLEARLY, RIGHT WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Five hundred days. A line heard on day ten can come back differently on day four hundred. Same words, new weight. The next three discourses take yesterday's verse and pass it through four monks. One teaches it from memory. Two first hear of it from a deity, and don't know it. And one explains it when the Buddha leaves it unexplained. It's almost a study in how a teaching travels.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `SAME WORDS, NEW WEIGHT.` → `ONE VERSE, FOUR MONKS.`

segments.voice: In the hundred and thirty-second discourse, Ananda teaches the verse and its explanation to the monks in the assembly hall. The Buddha later asks who taught it, and confirms Ananda got it right. Ananda had heard it and kept it. In the hundred and thirty-third, a monk named Samiddhi goes to bathe at some hot springs near Rajagaha. A deity appears at night and asks: do you know the bhaddekaratta verse? No. Learn it, says the deity. So Samiddhi asks the Buddha, who recites only the verse and goes inside. The monks are left with a short poem and no explanation. They go to Mahakaccana, known for unpacking the Buddha's brief sayings. He explains it through the senses: you chase the past when your mind is bound by desire to what the eye once saw, thinking, such was my eye, such were the sights. You build on the future when you set your heart on what the eye will see. The Buddha hears this and says: if you'd asked me, I'd have explained it the same way. In the hundred and thirty-fourth, a monk named Lomasakangiya is asked about the verse by a deity named Candana. He doesn't know it. But Candana does, and recites it, saying the Buddha once taught it to the gods. So Lomasakangiya walks all the way to Savatthi to hear it properly. Three discourses, three ways of meeting the same few lines, and one line they all carry: do today what needs doing, with energy. In Pali, ajja eva kiccam atappam: today itself, the ardent effort.
screen: `ANANDA: HEARD IT AND KEPT IT` · `MAHAKACCANA UNPACKS THE SENSES` · `LOMASAKANGIYA WALKS TO LEARN IT` · `TODAY ITSELF, THE EFFORT` · then, large: `TODAY, THE EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Silently and slowly, say a short version of the verse in your own words, to keep it the way Ananda kept his, one line with each out-breath: don't chase the past; don't pin hopes on the future; see what's here; today, the effort. Then rest in whatever is actually here between the lines.
Atappa. Ardor, keen effort: the line that Ananda, Mahakaccana and Lomasakangiya each carried on, as they met the bhaddekaratta verse. Today's word.
Your line: today, the effort. Five hundred days in, the effort is still only ever today's. Day five hundred, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics memorize and chant short verses and study the commentaries that explain them; the bhaddekaratta verse is among those chanted in some communities.

fork.setup: the Buddha recites a short verse and goes into his dwelling without explaining it. you're one of the monks. what do the monks in MN 133 do?
options: go to Mahakaccana and ask him to explain it.
fork.reveal: they go to Mahakaccana, known for expanding the Buddha's brief sayings, and the Buddha approves his explanation.

original.note: Pali atappa: ardor, keen effort. from the verse: today itself, the ardent effort.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse means one thing, and you learn it once.
what it means: in three discourses, four monks meet the same verse, and each carries it on.

what a scholar hears: MN 132–134 frame the bhaddekaratta verse with different speakers, and MN 133 is one of several suttas where Mahakaccana expands a brief saying (uddesa) into a full exposition (vibhanga).
recall: a thicket, a tangle hard to see into
guess: a vow kept for a whole lifetime
a calm that needs no effort

chat.says: Why would the same short verse need three whole discourses?
options: It travels: Ananda keeps it, Mahakaccana explains it, Lomasakangiya walks far to hear it.
Each discourse corrects the verse, until the Buddha writes down a final version.
The monks argued over it, and the Buddha said each explanation they gave was wrong.
chat.meaning: Ananda teaches it, Mahakaccana unpacks it and the Buddha approves, and Lomasakangiya walks to Savatthi to learn it properly.

Mahakaccana.meaning: a monk known for unpacking the Buddha's brief sayings

Samiddhi.meaning: a monk who learned of the verse from a deity

Lomasakangiya.meaning: a monk who walked to Savatthi to hear the verse

Rajagaha.meaning: a royal city, with hot springs nearby

notes: MN 132–134 paraphrased. Confirm: Samiddhi at the Tapoda hot springs near Rajagaha; Lomasakangiya among the Sakyans, asked by the deity Candana; Candana says the Buddha taught the verse among the Tavatimsa gods.
The Pali 'ajj' eva kiccam atappam' is cited from memory of the verse; confirm spelling (ajjeva kiccam atappam).
